section_summary: This section consists chiefly of State Department filing and cross-reference sheets paired with diplomatic telegrams on Japanese military movements during the 1932 Shanghai conflict and in Manchuria. It traces the staged Japanese evacuation of positions around Shanghai, the restoration of Chinese police and civil control, and negotiations over the armistice and a proposed round-table conference. At the same time, reports describe Japanese reinforcements moving through Harbin and along the Songhua River and Chinese Eastern Railway, where forces associated with Ma Zhanshan and other commanders resisted the Japanese advance.

subfiles.title: File note on Japanese troops landing in the International Settlement
subfiles.about: A filing note refers to Cunningham's telegram reporting a Japanese landing at the wayside wharf in the Shanghai International Settlement.
subfiles.summary: The sheet directs readers to telegram no. 50 in file 793.94/4186. Its abstract records that Japanese troops were reported to have landed inside the International Settlement.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 50: Japanese landing and conditions at Shanghai
subfiles.about: Cunningham reports quiet fronts at Zhabei and Wusong and the landing of about twelve thousand Japanese troops in the International Settlement.
subfiles.summary: Cunningham continues his daily report on the Shanghai fighting, describing both the Zhabei and Wusong fronts as comparatively quiet. He reports that approximately twelve thousand Japanese troops had landed at the wayside wharf in the International Settlement and states that the message was repeated to the Legation and Nanking.

subfiles.title: File note on Lieutenant Brom's report about Japanese forces
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a report by Naval Attaché Lieutenant C. C. Brom on Japanese troop movements and equipment.
subfiles.summary: This filing note points to despatch no. 1385 in file 793.94/4649. The referenced report contains Lieutenant Brom's observations concerning the movement and equipment of Japanese forces.

subfiles.title: File note on Japanese deployments from Tientsin
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a Tientsin despatch about Japanese detachments sent to Shanhaiguan and an enlarged garrison at Peiping.
subfiles.summary: The filing note points to a despatch in the Tientsin post records. Its abstract says that small Japanese detachments had periodically left Tientsin for Shanhaiguan and that the Peiping garrison had also been increased.

subfiles.title: Despatch extract on Japanese movements near Shanhaiguan
subfiles.about: Lockhart reports Japanese detachments from Tientsin and rumors of operations along the railway between Shanhaiguan and Tanggu.
subfiles.summary: Japanese troops sent to Shanhaiguan and Peiping were reportedly drawn from the forces quartered in the Tientsin concession. Information suggested possible operations along the railway between Shanhaiguan and Tanggu, but Lockhart emphasized that the report lacked confirmation.

subfiles.title: File note on Japanese and Chinese troop strength
subfiles.about: The sheet records an estimate of about 51,000 Japanese troops in China and uncertainty over Chinese troop dispositions.
subfiles.summary: This filing note refers to a telegram in file 793.94/4717. Its abstract estimates Japanese strength in China at approximately 51,000 while noting that reliable information on Chinese deployments was difficult to obtain.

subfiles.title: File note on contemplated Japanese withdrawal from Shanghai
subfiles.about: The sheet notes that the Tokyo War Office was considering withdrawing some troops from Shanghai.
subfiles.summary: The referenced telegram reported active consideration in Tokyo of a partial withdrawal. At the time of the report, Japanese headquarters at Shanghai had received no order to begin it.

subfiles.title: Telegram: Joint situation reports nos. 6 and 7
subfiles.about: Johnson reports stabilization of the Shanghai front and orders for the Eleventh Division and Twenty-fourth Mixed Brigade to return to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese Fourteenth Division had entered the line, but activity was limited largely to minor clashes with cavalry patrols and the Chinese appeared prepared to remain on the defensive. Japanese headquarters said Tokyo was considering withdrawals, and orders subsequently arrived for the Eleventh Division and Twenty-fourth Mixed Brigade to return to Japan.

subfiles.title: File note on the beginning of Japanese withdrawal from Shanghai
subfiles.about: A poorly preserved filing note records an ambassador's statement that withdrawal of Japanese forces from Shanghai had begun.
subfiles.summary: The surviving text summarizes a report on the removal of Japanese forces from Shanghai. It states that an ambassador believed the withdrawal was already under way, but the source and date are not legible.

subfiles.title: File note on Colonel Drysdale's report of an embarkation
subfiles.about: The sheet summarizes Colonel Drysdale's report that a Japanese brigade had begun embarking.
subfiles.summary: The abstract says that part of a Japanese brigade embarked on March 18. The remainder was scheduled to leave on the following day.

subfiles.title: Telegram: Twenty-fourth Mixed Brigade embarking for Moji
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, forwarding Colonel Drysdale's report
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, Washington, for the War Department
subfiles.about: Drysdale reports that the Twenty-fourth Mixed Brigade was embarking for Moji and would be followed by the Eleventh Division.
subfiles.summary: Conditions remained quiet along both Shanghai fronts. One and one-half battalions of the Twenty-fourth Mixed Brigade embarked for Moji, with the remainder scheduled to follow the next day and the Eleventh Division to depart later.

subfiles.title: File note on Joint Situation Report no. 11
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a situation report stating that the embarkation of a Japanese mixed brigade continued.
subfiles.summary: This note identifies joint situation report no. 11. Its abstract highlights the continuing departure of a Japanese mixed brigade from Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Telegram: Joint Situation Report no. 11
subfiles.about: Johnson reports continued Japanese embarkation and a Chinese protest over Japanese aircraft operating beyond the Shirakawa patrol zone.
subfiles.summary: The embarkation of a Japanese mixed brigade for Japan was continuing. The Nineteenth Route Army protested Japanese flights beyond the Shirakawa patrol zone, although claims that aircraft fire had injured civilians could not be verified.

subfiles.title: File note on Japanese troop arrivals at Harbin
subfiles.about: The sheet records the arrival at Harbin of five echelons of Japanese troops from the south.
subfiles.summary: The note points to telegram no. 276 in file 793.94/4420. Its abstract says that five Japanese troop echelons reached Harbin on February 25.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 276: Japanese reinforcements at Harbin
subfiles.from: Mahlon F. Perkins, forwarding the American Consul General at Harbin
subfiles.about: The Harbin consul reports Japanese troop arrivals and warns of complications with the Soviet Union if they move toward the frontier.
subfiles.summary: Five echelons of Japanese troops had arrived from the south, and further arrivals were expected. Although conditions on the eastern railway line were said to be less serious than Japanese propaganda suggested, the military appeared determined to deploy troops there, creating a risk of complications with Soviet Russia.

subfiles.title: File note on Japan's proposed Shanghai truce terms
subfiles.about: The sheet summarizes Japan's position that withdrawal from Shanghai should remain voluntary and outside neutral control.
subfiles.summary: The filing note refers to telegram no. 362. Its abstract emphasizes Japanese opposition to neutral control over the withdrawal of its Shanghai forces.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 362: Japanese objections to the Shanghai truce draft
subfiles.about: Perkins forwards Japanese press reports detailing the government's proposed truce terms and objections to neutral supervision.
subfiles.summary: Nippon Dempo reported that Japan wanted a voluntary withdrawal to the Shanghai–Wusong line, flexible policing arrangements, and a later round-table conference intended to secure a broader peace. Rengo described objections to language permitting neutral military attachés to supervise withdrawal and to provisions placing the evacuated zone solely under Chinese police. Japanese officials distinguished a tactical withdrawal for suspending hostilities from the eventual return of the army to Japan and insisted that China explicitly accept a round-table conference.

subfiles.title: File note on Japanese troop strength at Tientsin
subfiles.about: The sheet notes that two hundred Japanese troops arrived in Tientsin but that comparable departures left the total garrison unchanged.
subfiles.summary: About two hundred additional Japanese troops reportedly arrived on February 14. Because approximately the same number had gone elsewhere, Lockhart found no substantial net increase in Japanese strength at Tientsin.

subfiles.title: File note on replacement of General Tamon at Harbin
subfiles.about: The sheet reports that General Hirose and his division would replace General Tamon at Harbin.
subfiles.summary: This filing note abstracts a telegram concerning Japanese command changes at Harbin. General Tamon's troops were to be relieved by General Hirose's division.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 444: Change of Japanese divisions at Harbin
subfiles.from: Mahlon F. Perkins, forwarding the American Consul General at Harbin
subfiles.about: The Harbin consul reports the impending replacement of General Tamon and his troops by General Hirose's division.
subfiles.summary: The American Consul General at Harbin stated that General Tamon and his troops would soon leave their assignment. General Hirose and his division were designated to replace them.

subfiles.title: File note on the projected withdrawal from Shanghai
subfiles.about: The sheet records a statement that Japanese troops would leave Shanghai once order was restored, possibly within six months.
subfiles.summary: The note concerns the eventual removal of Japanese forces from Shanghai. An undersecretary reportedly predicted withdrawal after the restoration of order and suggested a period of as much as six months.

subfiles.title: File note on the Yoda Brigade's movement to Harbin
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to an announcement that the Yoda Brigade had left Changchun for Harbin.
subfiles.summary: This note points to telegram no. 474 in the Manchuria files. Its abstract records the northward departure of the Yoda Brigade from Changchun.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 474: Transfer of the Yoda Brigade
subfiles.from: Mahlon F. Perkins, forwarding the American Consul General at Mukden
subfiles.about: The Mukden consul reports that the Yoda Brigade moved from Changchun to Harbin after an earlier transfer from Jinzhou.
subfiles.summary: Japanese headquarters announced that the Yoda Brigade had departed Changchun for Harbin. It had previously moved from Jinzhou through Tongliao and Siping, leaving detachments along the route, and was replaced at Jinzhou by the Hirosaki Brigade.

subfiles.title: File note on northward Japanese movements in Manchuria
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to confidential information that Japanese troops were moving north in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies a confidential telegram on Japanese deployments. Its brief abstract says that substantial forces were moving toward northern Manchuria.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 495: Japanese reinforcements moving north
subfiles.from: Mahlon F. Perkins, forwarding the American Consul General at Mukden
subfiles.about: A confidential Mukden report describes the movement of Japanese divisions and reinforcements into eastern Jilin and northern Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The Korea Division at Jinzhou had reportedly been relieved by the Hirosaki Division and sent into eastern Jilin, where it was joined by reinforcements from northern Korea. Japanese authorities regarded the situation in northern Manchuria as serious and had requested still more troops, while withholding detailed information about the movements.

subfiles.title: File note on Japanese river transport in Manchuria
subfiles.about: The sheet records the movement of Japanese troops down the Songhua River in steamers escorted by gunboats.
subfiles.summary: This filing note refers to telegram no. 499. Its abstract highlights the use of armed river transport in the Japanese advance north of Harbin.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 499: Fighting and Japanese advances north and east of Harbin
subfiles.from: Mahlon F. Perkins, forwarding a Reuters report from Harbin
subfiles.about: A Reuters report describes damaged railways, Japanese advances toward Mudanjiang, river-borne troop movements, and arrests connected with an alleged plot against the Lytton Commission.
subfiles.summary: Anti-Manchukuo troops, reportedly including forces under Ma Zhanshan, had destroyed bridges on the Huhai Railway, while Japanese troops advanced toward Mudanjiang and occupied towns north of Harbin. Fangzheng was still being defended, and Japanese soldiers were traveling down the Songhua River in escorted steamers. Chinese, Koreans, and Russians were among those arrested over an alleged conspiracy to kill members of the Lytton Commission.

subfiles.title: File note on resistance along the Huhai Railway
subfiles.about: The sheet says Heilongjiang troops supporting Ma Zhanshan held the railway north of Hulan against Japanese forces.
subfiles.summary: The filing note refers to telegram no. 501. Its abstract describes Chinese efforts to block a Japanese advance along the Huhai Railway.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 501: Military situation around Harbin
subfiles.from: Mahlon F. Perkins, forwarding the American Consul General at Harbin
subfiles.about: The Harbin consul reports fighting on the Huhai Railway, Songhua River, and Chinese Eastern Railway east of Harbin.
subfiles.summary: Heilongjiang troops supporting Ma Zhanshan controlled the Huhai Railway north of Hulan while Japanese forces entrenched near Songpu. Other Japanese troops advanced by steamer on the Songhua River and reached the Mudan River east of Hailin, where Wang Delin's men held the line toward Pogranichnaya. Former Jilin troops occupied Bin County and moved toward Harbin and Mao'ershan amid extensive railway damage.

subfiles.title: File note on the May 6 withdrawal from Shanghai
subfiles.about: The sheet notes the withdrawal of one Japanese battalion from each of several Shanghai-area positions.
subfiles.summary: The filing note refers to telegram no. 222. Its abstract says that Japanese forces began withdrawing one battalion apiece from designated localities on May 6.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 222: First withdrawals of the Third Division
subfiles.about: Cunningham reports Japanese battalions leaving Nanxiang, Luodian, Liuhe, and Jiading for embarkation at Wusong.
subfiles.summary: One infantry battalion was being withdrawn from each of Nanxiang, Luodian, Liuhe, and Jiading to Wusong for embarkation to Dalian, as part of the withdrawal of roughly 24,000 men of the Third Division. Chinese police from Nanking were expected to assume control of the evacuated districts under the peace agreement, with additional police coming from Peiping.

subfiles.title: File note on Wang Tien-chung's force in Manchuria
subfiles.about: The sheet describes a Japanese-assisted force in Manchuria under Wang Tien-chung.
subfiles.summary: Wang Tien-chung, formerly an officer under Chang Tsung-ch'ang, commanded a force operating in Manchuria. The group consisted largely of former bandits and had reportedly been organized with Japanese assistance during the preceding autumn.

subfiles.title: File note on the completion of the first evacuation phase
subfiles.about: The sheet reports Drysdale's observation of the peaceful evacuation of Luodian and the return of Chinese police.
subfiles.summary: The note refers to telegram no. 235. It states that the first phase of the evacuation ended at Luodian and that the Japanese made further withdrawals conditional on subsequent developments.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 235: Luodian evacuated
subfiles.about: Cunningham reports Drysdale's observation of the Japanese evacuation of Luodian and the scheduled transition to Chinese control.
subfiles.summary: Colonel Drysdale personally observed the Japanese evacuation and Chinese resumption of control, including the peaceful entry of Chinese police into Luodian. This completed the first evacuation phase; no date had yet been announced for the next withdrawal from the Yinghsiang–Dachang–Zhenru position.

subfiles.title: File note on Japanese unit withdrawals of May 9
subfiles.about: The sheet records the withdrawal of complete Japanese units and anticipates further departures.
subfiles.summary: This note summarizes a telegram concerning Japanese compliance with the evacuation arrangements. Complete units were withdrawn on May 9, with additional withdrawals to follow later.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 232: Evacuation of Liuhe, Jiading, Nanxiang, and Luodian
subfiles.about: Cunningham details the transfer of evacuated towns to Chinese police and civil administrators under the May 5 agreement.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese delegation stated that complete units had left Liuhe, Jiading, and Nanxiang and that Luodian would be evacuated at noon on May 10. Four hundred special police from Nanking were available to enter the towns, accompanied by Chinese civil officials and interpreters. Cunningham requested guidance on how much detail to report as the first three paragraphs of the Sino-Japanese agreement were implemented.

subfiles.title: File note on completion of the Japanese army evacuation
subfiles.about: The sheet records the evacuation of Jiangwan, restoration of Chinese control, and embarkation of the last Japanese army units.
subfiles.summary: The filing note refers to telegram no. 273. It states that Chinese authorities resumed control of the Jiangwan area on May 29 and that the last Japanese army units embarked on May 31.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 273: Final army embarkations and remaining naval forces
subfiles.about: Cunningham reports completion of the army evacuation while Japanese naval forces and gendarmes retained several Shanghai positions.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese army completed its evacuation of area no. 2 at Jiangwan, and its last units embarked for Japan. Japanese naval landing forces nevertheless retained the Wusong barracks area, Yinghsiang, and Zhabei with gendarmes or marines. Chinese forces reoccupied Longhua with two hundred gendarmes of the Sixth Regiment.

subfiles.title: File note on the May 9 evacuation of three towns
subfiles.about: The sheet reports complete Japanese evacuation of Liuhe, Jiading, and Nanxiang and the restoration of Chinese control.
subfiles.summary: The filing note abstracts a War Department report. It emphasizes that the transfer of the three localities to Chinese control occurred without reported trouble.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 233: Drysdale's report on the first evacuation line
subfiles.from: Edwin S. Cunningham, forwarding Colonel Drysdale's report
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, Washington, for the War Department
subfiles.about: Drysdale reports the evacuation of Liuhe, Jiading, and Nanxiang and the planned evacuation of Luodian.
subfiles.summary: Japanese forces fully evacuated Liuhe, Jiading, and Nanxiang, after which Chinese authorities resumed control without incident. Luodian was to follow, leaving a Japanese defensive line through Yinghsiang, Dachang, and Zhenru. The Fourteenth Division was ordered to Manchuria, while a mountain-artillery regiment was returning to Japan.

subfiles.title: File note on Lo Wen-kan's statement about the peace agreement
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to Lo Wen-kan's expression of confidence that Japanese troops would withdraw from Shanghai.
subfiles.summary: The filing note points to telegram no. 511. Its abstract highlights the Chinese Foreign Minister's confidence that Japanese troops would return to their pre-January 28 defensive positions.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 511: Lo Wen-kan explains the Shanghai agreement
subfiles.from: Mahlon F. Perkins, forwarding a Kuo Wen report from Nanking
subfiles.about: Lo Wen-kan defends the Shanghai peace settlement and discusses its implications for Manchuria and relations with the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Lo expressed confidence that the Japanese would withdraw and said Chinese negotiators had defeated demands for a round-table conference, a Shanghai free port, extension of the Settlement, and suppression of the anti-Japanese boycott. He described compromises over the withdrawal zone and rejected restrictions on Chinese troops south of Suzhou Creek and in Pudong. Although the agreement did not secure immediate total withdrawal, he called it the best available settlement and said China would next address Manchuria; he also warned that recent Soviet actions hindered restoration of Sino-Soviet relations.

subfiles.title: File note on a change in Japanese command at Tientsin
subfiles.about: The sheet reports Kashii's departure, Nakamura's succession, and growing Japanese opposition to military operations at Shanghai.
subfiles.summary: Lieutenant General Kashii reportedly left for Japan on March 10 and was succeeded by Major General K. Nakamura. The note also records increasing opposition within Japan to the Shanghai military campaign.

subfiles.title: File note on Japanese activity at Shanhaiguan
subfiles.about: The sheet says reported Japanese military activity at Shanhaiguan consisted of minor maneuvers and that the garrison had not increased.
subfiles.summary: The note abstracts a Tientsin telegram on conditions at Shanhaiguan. It places the Japanese garrison at roughly two hundred and characterizes its recent actions as demonstrations rather than a major buildup.

subfiles.title: Telegram: Japanese and Manchukuo actions at Shanhaiguan
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, Washington, and American Legation in China
subfiles.about: Acheson reports demonstrations by the Japanese garrison and the brief occupation of Shanhaiguan station by Manchukuo police.
subfiles.summary: Japanese officials attributed reports of military activity to minor maneuvers, and independent information indicated that the two-hundred-man garrison had not been reinforced. After the Chinese commander refused to sign a statement admitting inability to keep order, one hundred uniformed Manchukuo police under a Japanese officer occupied the railway station. They withdrew twenty-four hours later following a protest by the British railway official on duty.

subfiles.title: File note on the cabinet decision to evacuate Shanghai
subfiles.about: The sheet records a Reuters report that Japan would withdraw its expeditionary force from Shanghai within a month.
subfiles.summary: The note refers to telegram no. 524. Its abstract says that only a small bluejacket force would remain to protect Japanese residents after the army's withdrawal.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 524: Japanese cabinet orders complete Shanghai withdrawal
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, forwarding a Reuters report from Tokyo
subfiles.about: A Japanese Foreign Office spokesman announces the withdrawal of the Shanghai expeditionary force and the retention of only a small naval guard.
subfiles.summary: The cabinet decided to remove the entire expeditionary force within a month, return the Ninth Division to Kanazawa, and reduce Japanese strength at Shanghai to its pre-January level. Some troops would return to Japan and others move to Manchuria, while only a small bluejacket force would remain. The spokesman linked the decision to world opinion but warned that other powers would bear responsibility if withdrawal endangered Shanghai.

subfiles.title: File note on the Utsunomiya Division's movement north
subfiles.about: The sheet records the movement of Utsunomiya Division troops from Dalian through Harbin toward Sanxing.
subfiles.summary: The note points to telegram no. 527 in the Manchuria files. Its abstract describes the transfer northward of Japanese troops formerly stationed at Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 527: Utsunomiya Division deployed against bandits
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, forwarding the American Consul General at Mukden
subfiles.about: The Mukden consul reports the movement of Utsunomiya Division troops to Sanxing for a major campaign in northern Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese Consul General stated that troops from the Utsunomiya Division were moving from Dalian through Harbin to Sanxing. Together with other forces and the Tamon Division at Jilin, they were to conduct an extensive campaign against so-called bandits before growing crops provided cover. The volume of troop traffic led the South Manchuria Railway to suspend acceptance of commercial freight between Dalian and Jinzhou.

subfiles.title: File note on Joint Commission notice of full withdrawal
subfiles.about: The sheet records the Japanese delegation's statement that the entire army would leave Shanghai within about a month.
subfiles.summary: The filing note refers to telegram no. 240. It summarizes an oral notice delivered through the Sino-Japanese Joint Commission.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 240: Japanese delegation promises withdrawal by June 10
subfiles.about: Cunningham reports an official oral assurance that the Japanese army would leave the Shanghai area by about June 10.
subfiles.summary: At a meeting in the American Consulate General, the Japanese delegation orally informed the Chinese delegation that the entire army in the Shanghai area would be withdrawn within about a month. June 10 was given as the latest anticipated date, and formal notice to the Joint Commission was expected shortly.

subfiles.title: File note on Chinese conditions for a round-table conference
subfiles.about: The sheet says China would not attend a Shanghai round-table conference until Japanese forces withdrew in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The filing note refers to telegram no. 529. Its abstract presents the Chinese position that Japanese troops first had to retire into the Manchurian railway zone.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 529: Chinese position on broader negotiations
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, forwarding Reuters reports
subfiles.about: Reuters reports that China viewed the Shanghai armistice as only a partial settlement and would not negotiate political issues while Japanese troops occupied Chinese territory.
subfiles.summary: Chinese officials said no Shanghai round-table conference could occur until Japanese troops in Manchuria withdrew into the railway zone. They characterized the Shanghai settlement as only one part of the wider Sino-Japanese conflict. A separate Shanghai report predicted that troop withdrawal would begin around May 20 and finish before the end of the month, after which General Shirakawa would be relieved and the force reorganized.

subfiles.title: File note on Imperial authority over Japanese army movements
subfiles.about: The sheet records the Japanese position that an Imperial withdrawal order could not be countermanded.
subfiles.summary: This filing note refers to telegram no. 530. Its abstract emphasizes that movement of the Imperial Army was determined by Imperial authority rather than by petitions from Japanese residents at Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 530: Araki on the Shanghai withdrawal order
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, forwarding a Rengo report from Tokyo
subfiles.about: War Minister Araki says the withdrawal order is irrevocable and reports military deliberations on policy after the evacuation.
subfiles.summary: Araki responded to a petition from Japanese residents at Shanghai by saying that Imperial authority governed army movements and that the withdrawal order could not be rescinded. He nevertheless promised that the army would not abandon residents if conditions again became dangerous. The Supreme Military Council considered post-withdrawal policy toward Shanghai, both northern and southern Manchuria, Soviet Russia, and the League of Nations.

subfiles.title: File note on Japanese troop movements in Manchuria
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a report on continuing Japanese troop movements through Harbin.
subfiles.summary: The filing note points to telegram no. 531. Its subject is the deployment of Japanese reinforcements in northern Manchuria.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 531: Japanese advance from Harbin
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, forwarding the American Consul General at Harbin
subfiles.about: The Harbin consul reports Japanese forces moving east and down the Songhua River while Ma Zhanshan threatens the western railway line.
subfiles.summary: Japanese troops continued arriving from the south and were sent east along the Chinese Eastern Railway or down the Songhua River toward Sanxing, fighting former Jilin forces and brigands en route. The railway's western line was threatened near Anda by fortified troops of Ma Zhanshan, who appeared committed to armed resistance against the Japanese advance in Heilongjiang.

subfiles.title: File note on the withdrawal of Japanese bluejackets
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to Drysdale's observation of Japanese bluejackets leaving an evacuated Shanghai district.
subfiles.summary: The note points to telegram no. 245. Its abstract records the withdrawal of Japanese naval personnel and the peaceful restoration of Chinese police control.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 245: Chinese police resume control south of the railway
subfiles.about: Cunningham reports the withdrawal of Japanese bluejackets and Drysdale's replacement by Lieutenant Soule on the Joint Commission.
subfiles.summary: Colonel Drysdale witnessed Japanese bluejackets withdraw from the portion of Zhabei south of the railway and saw five hundred Peiping police assume control without incident. Drysdale was to leave for Peiping, with Lieutenant Robert H. Soule replacing him as the American member of the Joint Commission.

subfiles.title: File note on the scheduled evacuation of Dachang
subfiles.about: The sheet says Dachang would be evacuated on May 17 and notes Chinese requests concerning railway repairs.
subfiles.summary: The filing note refers to telegram no. 246. Its abstract records both the next Japanese withdrawal and Chinese efforts to regain access to railway lines in the evacuated area.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 246: Arrangements for the Dachang evacuation
subfiles.about: Cunningham reports Japanese notice of the Dachang evacuation and Chinese preparations to take over the area and railway lines.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese informed Chinese representatives that Dachang would be evacuated at one o'clock on May 17 and requested prior contact between the two sides. China notified Japan of the personnel assigned to restore control and asked that the relevant railway lines also be evacuated so repairs and operations could resume.

subfiles.title: File note on the Japanese withdrawal from Dachang
subfiles.about: The sheet records the withdrawal of Japanese infantry from Dachang and the return of Chinese police.
subfiles.summary: The note refers to telegram no. 247. Its abstract states that Chinese police peacefully resumed control after the Japanese battalion departed.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 247: Lieutenant Soule observes the Dachang transfer
subfiles.about: Cunningham reports Soule's observation of a Japanese battalion leaving Dachang and Chinese police entering the district.
subfiles.summary: Lieutenant Soule personally witnessed one Japanese infantry battalion withdraw from Dachang and its immediate vicinity. One hundred fifty Chinese police from Nanking resumed control of the evacuated area without incident.

subfiles.title: File note on the scheduled withdrawal from Zhenru
subfiles.about: The sheet records Japanese notice that the defense units at Zhenru would withdraw on May 20.
subfiles.summary: This filing note refers to telegram no. 248. It identifies Zhenru and its station as the next positions scheduled for evacuation.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 248: Notice of the Zhenru evacuation
subfiles.about: Cunningham reports that Japanese Joint Commissioners scheduled withdrawal from Zhenru and Zhenru station for May 20.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese members of the Joint Commission formally notified their Chinese counterparts of the planned withdrawal. Japanese defense units at Zhenru and its railway station were scheduled to leave at one o'clock on May 20.

subfiles.title: File note on revised evacuation plans for Zhenru, Jiangwan, and Zhabei
subfiles.about: The sheet records the postponement of the Zhenru withdrawal and outlines planned withdrawals from Jiangwan and Zhabei.
subfiles.summary: The filing note refers to telegram no. 249. Its abstract notes that the Zhenru evacuation was deferred until May 23 and that further army and naval withdrawals were being coordinated.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 249: Revised Shanghai evacuation schedule
subfiles.about: Cunningham reports revised dates for withdrawals from Zhenru, Jiangwan, and Zhabei and discusses policing and railway arrangements.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese postponed withdrawal from Zhenru and its station until May 23, while planning to leave western Jiangwan on May 19 and most of Zhabei on May 23. Chinese delegates were asked to arrange the transfer of Zhabei with the Japanese naval landing party. The Japanese also complained that Dachang had not been taken over by the designated special police and requested a complete Chinese program for reopening railway lines.

subfiles.title: File note on the withdrawal from Jiangwan
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to Lieutenant Soule's observation of the Japanese withdrawal from Jiangwan and the return of Chinese police control.
subfiles.summary: This filing note introduces a telegram that continues beyond the supplied section. Its abstract states that Lieutenant Soule witnessed Japanese forces leave Jiangwan and Chinese police resume authority there.
